left.heading: WHAT IT IS:
left.body: Two protocols working together, already built into the device in your pocket.
left.draw: A phone sitting in the back pocket of a pair of jeans, with a small green padlock shield beside it.

right.heading: WHY IT PERSISTS:
right.body: It survives switching from mobile data to Wi-Fi without dropping the tunnel.
right.draw: A mobile mast labelled `4G / 5G` on the left and a Wi-Fi router on the right, joined by a pipe labelled `IKEV2 / IPSEC TUNNEL`.

how.heading: HOW IT WORKS
how.subtitle: Four design decisions that define the protocol.

cards.heading: TWO PROTOCOLS, NOT ONE
cards.body: IKEv2 negotiates the keys. IPsec ESP actually carries the data. Most people say one and mean both.
cards.draw: Two joined boxes, the left labelled `IKEV2 - KEYS` and the right labelled `ESP - DATA`, drawn with a single brace underneath spanning both.

cards.heading: LIVES IN THE KERNEL
cards.body: ESP is handled by the operating system's own network stack, so throughput stays high.
cards.draw: Three stacked boxes joined by downward arrows, labelled `USER SPACE (APPS)`, `KERNEL`, and `HARDWARE (NIC)`, with an envelope travelling down the chain.

cards.heading: MOBIKE FOR ROAMING
cards.body: A dedicated extension lets the tunnel survive an address change without renegotiating from scratch.
cards.draw: A person walking rightward carrying a phone, a long pipe running behind them from a mobile mast on the left to a Wi-Fi router on the right, unbroken.

cards.heading: ALREADY ON YOUR DEVICE
cards.body: Built into iOS, macOS, Windows and Android. No third-party client to install or trust.
cards.draw: A phone, a laptop and a tablet side by side, each showing a platform logo and each with a small blue ticked badge in its corner.

costs.heading: WHAT IT COSTS YOU
costs.subtitle: The price of a very large and very old specification.

cards.heading: FIXED PORTS
cards.body: UDP 500 and 4500, and nowhere else to go. Trivial for a network to block deliberately.
cards.draw: A brick wall with two pipes labelled `500` and `4500` hitting it and stopping dead, each marked with a red cross.

cards.heading: A HUGE NEGOTIATION SURFACE
cards.body: Many options, several of them historically weak, and plenty of ways to configure it badly.
cards.draw: A long list headed `AUTH / ENC / DH` naming `DES`, `3DES`, `AES-128`, `RC4`, `SHA-1` and more, four entries ringed in red, a question mark beside it.

cards.heading: NAT IS AWKWARD
cards.body: ESP has no port numbers of its own, so it has to be wrapped in UDP just to survive a home router.
cards.draw: A box labelled `ESP PACKET (NO PORTS)` above a larger box labelled `UDP ENVELOPE 4500` containing it, with an arrow down to a home router labelled `NAT`.

cards.heading: IMPLEMENTATIONS VARY
cards.body: The specification is enormous, so quality and interoperability differ sharply between vendors.
cards.draw: Three servers labelled `VENDOR A`, `VENDOR B` and `VENDOR C` joined by dashed lines, with one of the three links marked by a red cross.
